language.script_notes: English dominant; Inuktitut syllabics (a distinctive geometric script, unlike Latin letters) appear on signage in Nunavut specifically — a strong, unmistakable regional tell where visible.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Northwest Territories: black-and-white striped cylindrical bollards with two thick black bands — a distinctive regional tell.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Cylindrical with thick black-and-white stripes in the NWT.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Minimal to absent on the very limited road network.
road_furniture.line_paint: As national where roads are paved; many stretches are unpaved gravel.
road_furniture.curb_style: Essentially absent outside the handful of covered towns (Whitehorse, Yellowknife, Tuktoyaktuk, Iqaluit, Cambridge Bay).
road_furniture.km_marker_style: As national on the very limited highway network — the Dempster Highway (Yukon to NWT) and the Top of the World Highway are among the only long-distance routes with coverage.

architecture.roof_style: Simple, utilitarian buildings built to withstand extreme cold; raised/piled foundations common given permafrost.
architecture.wall_construction: Simple prefab/modular construction is the norm in remote northern communities; almost no dense urban development outside Whitehorse, Yellowknife and Iqaluit.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Often brightly painted buildings stand out deliberately against the white/grey Arctic landscape for visibility.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Small, isolated northern communities with colourful prefab housing; almost no continuous urban development; a Trekker-only path exists as far north as Ellesmere Island, showing glacial, rocky, desolate landscape — the northernmost Street View coverage in the world.

nature.vegetation: Boreal forest in the southern Yukon/NWT gives way to treeless Arctic tundra further north — low shrubs, lichen, moss; almost no trees in the northernmost covered areas (Tuktoyaktuk, Nunavut).
nature.terrain: Vast, sparsely populated Arctic and subarctic terrain; permafrost, tundra, and the Arctic Ocean coastline (Tuktoyaktuk); glaciers and rocky desolation at the northernmost extreme (Ellesmere Island).
nature.climate_signature: Cold, often snow-covered even outside peak winter; long horizon-to-horizon tundra views with essentially no trees in the northernmost imagery — visually unmistakable once recognized.

vehicles.plate_color: The Northwest Territories' famous polar-bear-shaped license plate is a completely unique, instantly recognizable North American design.
vehicles.plate_format: As national elsewhere; NWT's plate shape itself is the identifier.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: 4WD/AWD vehicles necessary given terrain and climate; snowmobiles common in winter.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Very limited, specific coverage: the Dempster and Top of the World Highways in Yukon; the Alberta border to Yellowknife and Fort McPherson to Tuktoyaktuk in the NWT (plus Tulita); only Iqaluit and Cambridge Bay in Nunavut, plus a Trekker path on Ellesmere Island.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Extremely sparse and specific — coverage exists only along a handful of named highways and in a few named towns; anywhere else in the North has no coverage at all.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Shared Arctic/subarctic terrain, similar isolation and tundra/boreal vegetation
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Canadian speed signage is in km/h and plates carry a Canadian territory design (including the NWT's unique polar-bear-shaped plate) rather than an Alaska US state plate; Nunavut's Inuktitut syllabic script is a distinctive, unmistakable regional tell absent in Alaska.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Same country, same national plate/bollard base style
confusion_set.tiebreaker: The North is treeless Arctic tundra with extremely sparse, isolated coverage; the other Canadian regions are forested, flat-farmed, or mountainous with dense continuous coverage — the emptiness itself is the tell.
